verdict.rationale: The proposition restates two clauses almost verbatim, and six anchors layer independent negation strategies that all converge on one saving figure. Acts 4:12 stacks "there is not in another no one the salvation" (ouk estin en allo oudeni he soteria), then "nor for a name is there other" (oude gar onoma estin heteron), with the substantival "other" (heteron, used here as a standalone noun), the universal scope "under heaven" (hypo ton ouranon), and the impersonal "it is necessary" (dei) plus the passive "to be saved" (sothenai). 1 Timothy 2:5 puts the numeral "one" (heis, G1520) on both "God" (theos) and "mediator" (mesites, G3316); querying the store, the word for mediator (mesites) occurs 6 times and 4 of them name Christ, the other 2 (in Galatians) name the law-mediator and never a rival saving mediator. Hebrews 7:25 adds "to save" (sozein) "to the uttermost" (eis to panteles, G3838) and "to intercede" (entygchanein, G1793) "through him" (di autou). John 14:6 closes with "no one comes to the Father except through me" (oudeis erchetai pros ton patera ei me di emou), the strongest exclusive in Koine Greek (the common Greek of the New Testament), and 1 Corinthians 3:11 says "another foundation no one is able to lay" (themelion allon oudeis dynatai theinai), identifying the one foundation as "Jesus Christ" (Iesous Christos). The vocabulary centers the GROUND of salvation on one figure and supplies no second saving name, mediator, or foundation.

scripture.reasoning: The verse text in the store reads "and there is not in another no one the salvation, nor for a name is there other under heaven the having-been-given among humans by which it is necessary to be saved us" (kai ouk estin en allo oudeni he soteria, oude gar onoma estin heteron hypo ton ouranon to dedomenon en anthropois en ho dei sothenai hemas). The first clause pairs the negation "not" (ouk) with the dative "no one" (oudeni, in the 'to/for no one' grammatical form) and the locative "in another" (en allo), denying saving efficacy to any other source. The second uses the substantival "other" (heteron, used as a standalone noun), the universal scope "under heaven" (hypo ton ouranon), the perfect passive participle "having been given" (to dedomenon, a completed action whose result still stands), and the impersonal "it is necessary" (dei) plus the aorist passive (completed past action, passive voice) infinitive "to be saved" (sothenai, G4982) to bind salvation to the single given name.

The store text reads "for one God, one also mediator of God and of humans, a human Christ Jesus" (heis gar theos, heis kai mesites theou kai anthropon, anthropos Christos Iesous). The numeral "one" (heis, G1520) modifies "God" (theos) then "mediator" (mesites) in tight parallel, and the appositive "a human Christ Jesus" (anthropos Christos Iesous) names the single occupant of the mediatorial office. A direct query of the lexical store shows the word for mediator (mesites, G3316) occurring 6 times in the canon: here, Galatians 3:19 and 3:20 (the mediator of the law, the figure of Moses), and Hebrews 8:6, 9:15, 12:24 (mediator of the new covenant, named Jesus, Iesous). Four of the six name Christ and none names a parallel saving mediator alongside him.

The store text reads "from which also to save to the uttermost he is able those approaching through him to God, always living to intercede on behalf of them" (hothen kai sozein eis to panteles dynatai tous proserchomenous di autou to theo, pantote zon eis to entygchanein hyper auton). The complete-degree phrase "to the uttermost" (eis to panteles, G3838, only 2 canon occurrences) qualifies the saving infinitive "to save" (sozein, G4982), and the approach to God runs "through him" (di autou, G1223 plus pronoun). Querying "to intercede" (entygchano, G1793), saving intercession on behalf of people is applied to Christ here and at Romans 8:34, and to the Spirit at Romans 8:27. The one human use, Romans 11:2 of Elijah, is pleading against Israel, not saving intercession, so the upward intercession that saves attaches only to Christ and the Spirit.

The store text reads "I am the way and the truth and the life, no one comes to the Father except through me" (ego eimi he hodos kai he aletheia kai he zoe, oudeis erchetai pros ton patera ei me di emou). The emphatic "I am" (ego eimi) with articular (carrying the article 'the') predicate nominatives (nouns completing an 'X is Y' statement) identifies Jesus as the singular access, and the construction "no one ... except" (oudeis ... ei me), the strongest exclusive in Koine Greek (the common Greek of the New Testament), with "through me" (di emou, G1223) matching the "through him" (di autou) of Hebrews 7:25 morpheme for morpheme (word-part for word-part), closes every alternate route to the Father. John 10:9, confirmed in the store as "I am the door, through me if anyone enters he will be saved" (ego eimi he thyra, di emou ean tis eiselthe sothesetai), repeats the "through me" (di emou) plus "he will be saved" (sothesetai) pairing.

The store text reads "for another foundation no one is able to lay beside the one being laid, which is Jesus Christ" (themelion gar allon oudeis dynatai theinai para ton keimenon, hos estin Iesous Christos). The pairing of "other" (allon) with "no one" (oudeis) and the modal "is able" (dynatai) forecloses the possibility of laying any other foundation, and the relative clause "which is Jesus Christ" (hos estin Iesous Christos) names the one foundation. This repeats the "other" (allon) plus "no one" (oudeis) foreclosure that Acts 4:12 and John 14:6 apply to the saving name and route, now applied to the saving foundation.

The store text reads "and this is the testimony, that life eternal he gave the God to us, and this the life in the Son of him is" (kai haute estin he martyria, hoti zoen aionion edoken ho theos hemin, kai haute he zoe en to huio autou estin). The aorist (completed past action) "he gave" (edoken, G1325) locates the gift, and the locative "in the Son" (en to huio) binds "eternal life" (zoe aionios, G2222 plus G0166) to the Son as its container, the same given-into-one logic that Acts 4:12 applies with "the having been given" (to dedomenon) to the saving name.

"The one having the Son has the life, the one not having the Son of God the life does not have" (ho echon ton huion echei ten zoen, ho me echon ton huion tou theou ten zoen ouk echei). The participial antithesis between "having" (echon) and "not having" (me echon), with the negations "not" (me) and "not" (ouk), excludes life from anyone lacking the Son, restating the exclusivity in terms of possession. The store cross-reference data ties this to John 3:36, "the one believing in the Son has eternal life" (ho pisteuon eis ton huion echei zoen aionion).

complicating_texts.resolution: "And the mediator of one is not, but God one is" (ho de mesites henos ouk estin, ho de theos heis estin) is the one place the noun "mediator" (mesites, G3316) is used without naming Christ. A direct query of the store shows the context: Galatians 3:19 says the law was given "by the hand of a mediator" (en cheiri mesitou, the figure of Moses), and 3:20 draws the abstract point that a mediator implies more than one party. This is the law-mediator, not a rival saving mediator. It does not posit a second go-between for salvation, so it sharpens rather than contradicts the "one mediator" (heis mesites) of 1 Timothy 2:5.

Within the same letter that names the "one mediator" (heis mesites), God is called "Savior of all humans, especially of believers" (soter panton anthropon, malista piston), and 1 Timothy 2:4 says God "wills all humans to be saved" (thelei pantas anthropous sothenai). These texts speak to the SCOPE and the divine will in salvation, not to its ground or channel. They do not name a saving figure other than the one mediator, so they leave the through-Christ ground intact while bearing on the separate question of how widely salvation extends.

The same pericope (passage) that names the "one mediator" (heis mesites) first commands "requests, prayers, intercessions, thanksgivings on behalf of all humans" (deeseis, proseuchas, enteuxeis, eucharistias hyper panton anthropon). The cognate (related word) "intercessions" (enteuxeis, related to G1793) shows horizontal intercession among believers is enjoined immediately before the one-mediator clause, so it is lexically distinct from the singular vertical mediation. The text sets its own limit and does not introduce a second mediator.

"In every nation the one fearing him and working righteousness is acceptable to him" (en panti ethnei ho phoboumenos auton kai ergazomenos dikaiosynen dektos auto estin) could be read as opening a non-Christ path, but the store text of Acts 10:43 has Peter declare "forgiveness of sins to receive through the name of him" (aphesin hamartion labein dia tou onomatos autou, forgiveness through his name). The God-fearer Cornelius still must hear and believe the name, so "acceptable" (dektos) marks readiness for the gospel, not an alternate saving route, and the Acts 4:12 "name" (onoma) constraint holds.

The store holds Job 9:33 in Hebrew as "there is no arbiter between us" (lo yesh beneinu mokiach). Job laments the absence of a go-between to lay a hand on both parties. The lament marks the very gap that the one-mediator vocabulary later fills in Christ, so it confirms rather than complicates the singular pattern. Note the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, LXX) rendering uses "mediator" (mesites), but the underlying Hebrew term is "arbiter" (mokiach), so the cross-testament link is by sense, not by the same lexeme (dictionary word form).

variant_units_examined.note: The SBLGNT text in the store carries an editorial siglum (textual marker) on "nor" (oude) before "for" (gar), but the double-negation pattern "there is not in another no one" (ouk estin en allo oudeni) and the "other name" (onoma heteron) clause that forbids any other saving name persists in all readings.

The store text marks the article "the" (ho) before "Jesus" (Iesous) with a siglum (textual marker), but no witness drops the exclusive "no one comes to the Father except through me" (oudeis erchetai pros ton patera ei me di emou) clause, so the exclusive force is uniform across the tradition.

The store text marks word-order variation around "the God to us" (ho theos hemin) after "he gave" (edoken), but the claim binding "eternal life" (zoen aionion) to the Son, "in the Son of him" (en to huio autou), is stable across witnesses.

variants.note: A direct store query found no VariantUnit or Reading nodes attached to any of the six anchor verses; the 116 ingested VariantUnit nodes all sit in the 3 John ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) sample window. ECM is not published for Acts, John, 1 Timothy, Hebrews, 1 Corinthians, or 1 John, so this is shadow status and no cited verse is flagged as materially contested for the exclusivity claim.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads "not in another no one" (ouk en allo oudeni), "other name" (onoma heteron), "one mediator" (heis mesites), "another foundation no one" (themelion allon oudeis), and "no one except through me" (oudeis ei me di emou) at face value. The layered negations, the numeric singularity of "one" (heis), and the modal foreclosure "is able to lay" (dynatai theinai) together close off any alternate saving name, mediator, or foundation. The verified "mediator" (mesites) distribution (4 of 6 occurrences naming Christ, the other 2 the law-mediator) supplies no rival saving go-between.

Holds Christ as the sole ontological (concerning being itself) ground of all salvation but argues some may be saved through him without explicit knowledge of his name, leaning on 1 Timothy 4:10 "Savior of all humans" (soter panton anthropon) and 1 Timothy 2:4 "wills all to be saved" (thelei pantas sothenai) for the breadth of the saving will. On the proposition as stated, salvation is through Christ, this lens still affirms, since it does not posit a second saving figure. It diverges only on the separate SCOPE question of whether the lexical tie of "salvation" (soteria) to the heard "name" (onoma) (Acts 4:12) and to having the Son (1 John 5:12) requires conscious knowledge, which the anchors press toward but do not settle in isolation.

hermeneutics.notes: The proposition states the GROUND of salvation (through Christ, one name, one mediator, one foundation), not the epistemic (concerning knowledge) condition for receiving it. On that ground both available lenses affirm. They diverge only on the separate inclusivism question of implicit faith and the scope of the saving will, which 1 Timothy 2:4 and 4:10 raise but the exclusivity anchors do not adjudicate on their own. The verdict is on the ground, where the vocabulary is decisive.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Salvation is given through one figure, named in Acts 4:12 as the only name under heaven by which people must be saved, and identified in 1 Timothy 2:5 as the single mediator between God and humanity.
stem_audit.notes: The question_id label "solus-christus" (Latin for 'Christ alone') and the Five Solas subcategory carry a Reformation-era taxonomy coding, so a tradition-neutral rephrasing is supplied for transparency. The stem TEXT itself is not preloaded: it restates Acts 4:12 (no other name) and 1 Timothy 2:5 (no other mediator) in the canon's own lexical terms, so the verdict was derived on the original stem and the neutralized_form is informational only. VERDICT-CHANGED: no, verdict unchanged from the prior file. "Affirms" remains true, confidence high, after direct store queries confirmed every anchor verse verbatim, grounded the full 6-occurrence "mediator" (mesites) distribution, and refined the "to intercede" (entygchano) claim.

lay_summary: The proposition restates two New Testament clauses almost word for word, and six checked passages converge on one lexical pattern. In Acts 4:12 Peter stacks negations. There is no salvation "in no one else" (en allo oudeni), and no other "name" (onoma) under heaven, given among humans, by which it is necessary to be saved. The Greek uses the substantival "other" (heteron, used as a standalone noun), the universal scope under heaven, and the impersonal "it is necessary" (dei) with the passive infinitive "to be saved" (sothenai) to bind salvation to one given name. In 1 Timothy 2:5 the numeral "one" (heis) appears twice. One God, one mediator, named as the man Christ Jesus. The precise term for mediator (mesites) occurs only six times in the whole canon. Four of those name Christ, and the other two describe the mediator of the law, never a second mediator for salvation. Hebrews 7:25 says he saves "to the uttermost" (eis to panteles) those who approach God "through him" (di autou), and lives to make intercession (entygchanein). That saving intercession is applied only to Christ and the Spirit. John 14:6 closes with the strongest exclusive in Koine Greek (the common Greek of the New Testament), "no one comes to the Father except through me" (oudeis erchetai pros ton patera ei me di emou), and the "through me" (di emou) matches Hebrews 7:25 word-part for word-part. 1 Corinthians 3:11 adds that no one can lay another foundation, "another foundation no one is able to lay" (themelion allon oudeis dynatai theinai), than the one which is Jesus Christ. 1 John 5:11-12 binds eternal life to the Son. The words center the GROUND of salvation on one figure and offer no second saving name, mediator, or foundation, which is why this lands as a clear yes. Where readers still divide is not the ground but the scope. Texts in the same letter call God the Savior of all people and say he wills all to be saved, so some argue a person might be saved through Christ without consciously knowing his name. The exclusivity words press against that gap, since salvation is tied to the heard name and to having the Son, but they speak to the ground, not to that separate scope question.

The verbatim verse text used to verify every anchor clause comes from SBLGNT-text, and the syntactic anchoring of the "one mediator" (heis mesites) and "not in no one" (ouk en oudeni) clauses relies on MACULA-Greek, so the composite citation set cannot be redistributed in bulk without rebuilding from purely public-domain and CC-BY sources.
